qt: to the Commission Sebastian Kruis (PfE) Subject:

Under the European Union-Latin America and the Caribbean (EU-LAC) Global Gateway Investment Agenda, Team Europe has committed over EUR 45 billion to Latin America and the Caribbean for the period until 2027. Meanwhile, the United States is rapidly expanding its economic and strategic footprint in Latin America, in sectors ranging from critical raw materials and nearshoring to ports and digital infrastructure. This is a competitive risk, but also an opportunity. Where US capital and corporate networks are already moving, EU investors can gain speed and scale by plugging into those flows rather than simply building parallel structures. EU companies, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), still report difficulties in identifying bankable projects and accessing support with project preparation in the region. 1.
How does the Commission assess the effect of intensified US investment in the region on delivery of the EU-LAC Global Gateway Investment Agenda, and where does it see possibilities for cooperation?
Which instruments allow EU investors and SMEs to access project pipelines, technical assistance and co-financing through regional development banks, such as the InterAmerican Development Bank?

Is the Commission willing to launch a pilot with the Inter-American Development Bank and existing business platforms in the Western Hemisphere to develop a joint pipeline of bankable projects, and under what conditions could such a facility operate from outside the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.11.2026) The EU and the US share common interests in ensuring a level playing field in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), based on fair and sustainable trade and socially responsible investment. Both have converging interests in strategic sectors, such as digital infrastructure and critical raw materials. Coordination can help maximise the impact of engagement, while pursuing Global Gateway objectives. The European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus1 (EFSD+) offers risk-sharing tools through European and regional development banks. Seventeen guarantee agreements are active in the region, accompanied by technical assistance for project preparation. EU investors, including small and medium-sized enterprises, can propose projects and access pipelines via their Team National through the Global Gateway Investment Hub2, which connects EU companies, Member States, and financial institutions to mobilise financial and non-financial support. The Latin American and Caribbean Investment Facility3 (LACIF) also provides grants and technical assistance. The Commission maintains an active collaboration with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), which receives financing in 14 ongoing blending projects under the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument (NDICI-Global Europe). The IDB also co-organises the EU-LAC Business Forums. Any new initiative would need to demonstrate added value, complement existing tools and comply with applicable EU rules.
